claim: The mammalian vomeronasal organ encodes pheromone information about gender, reproductive status, genetic background and individual differences.
source: The mammalian vomeronasal organ encodes pheromone information about gender, reproductive status, genetic background and individual differences.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by multiple citations in the manuscript and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: A sub-group of V1re clade members recognizes gender-identifying cues in female urine.
source: A sub-group of V1re clade members recognizes gender-identifying cues in female urine.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from single-cell RT-PCR and transgenic mouse experiments showing V1re receptors respond to female urine.

claim: Multiple members of the V1rj clade are cognate receptors for urinary estrus signals.
source: Multiple members of the V1rj clade are cognate receptors for urinary estrus signals, as well as for sulfated estrogen (SE) compounds.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data showing V1rj receptors respond to estrus urine and sulfated estrogens.

claim: Multiple members of the V1rj clade are cognate receptors for sulfated estrogen (SE) compounds.
source: Multiple members of the V1rj clade are cognate receptors for urinary estrus signals, as well as for sulfated estrogen (SE) compounds.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging experiments showing V1rj2 and V1rj3 respond to E1050 and E1103.

claim: The same cue activates multiple homologous receptors, suggesting redundancy in encoding female pheromone cues.
source: In both cases, the same cue activates multiple homologous receptors, suggesting redundancy in encoding female pheromone cues.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that multiple V1rj and V1re receptors respond to the same stimuli.

claim: Neither gender-specific cues nor SEs alone are sufficient to promote courtship behavior in male mice.
source: Neither gender-specific cues nor SEs alone are sufficient to promote courtship behavior in male mice, whereas robust courtship behavior can be induced when the two cues are applied together.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assays showing that T16 or SE alone do not induce mounting, but together they do.

claim: Robust courtship behavior can be induced when gender-specific cues and SEs are applied together.
source: Neither gender-specific cues nor SEs alone are sufficient to promote courtship behavior in male mice, whereas robust courtship behavior can be induced when the two cues are applied together.
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral experiments showing T16+SE induces mounting comparable to estrus urine.

claim: Integrated action of different female cues is required in pheromone-triggered mating behavior.
source: Thus, integrated action of different female cues is required in pheromone-triggered mating behavior.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the behavioral data showing synergistic effects of combined cues.

claim: These results suggest a gating mechanism in the vomeronasal circuit in promoting specific innate behavior.
source: These results suggest a gating mechanism in the vomeronasal circuit in promoting specific innate behavior.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the requirement for both cues to induce behavior.

claim: Pheromones play an essential role in reproductive behaviors.
source: Pheromones play an essential role in reproductive behaviors.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field supported by citation (Wyatt, 2003).

claim: Sexually mature animals respond to pheromone signals from potential mates with endocrine changes and ritualistic action patterns.
source: Sexually mature animals respond to pheromone signals from potential mates with endocrine changes and ritualistic action patterns (Wyatt, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wyatt, 2003.

claim: Reproductive behaviors are not simple reflexes but complex neural processes modulated by multiple factors.
source: In spite of their innate nature, reproductive behaviors are not simple reflexes. They are complex neural processes that are modulated not only by the reproductive status of the animal (e.g., hormonal states, social ranks and past experiences), but also the status of potential mates and environmental factors such as the presence of predators (Tinbergen, 1951).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tinbergen, 1951 and represents established knowledge.

claim: The vomeronasal organ (VNO) is the major sensory organ responsible for pheromone detection in mammalian species.
source: Vomeronasal organ (VNO), the major sensory organ responsible for pheromone detection in mammalian species, expresses more than 300 vomeronasal receptors (VRs) (Dulac and Axel, 1995; Herrada and Dulac, 1997; Matsunami and Buck, 1997; Ryba and Tirindelli, 1997; Dulac and Torello, 2003; Shi and Zhang, 2007; Young and Trask, 2007; Liberles et al., 2009; Riviere et al., 2009; Liberles, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The VNO expresses more than 300 vomeronasal receptors (VRs).
source: Vomeronasal organ (VNO), the major sensory organ responsible for pheromone detection in mammalian species, expresses more than 300 vomeronasal receptors (VRs) (Dulac and Axel, 1995; Herrada and Dulac, 1997; Matsunami and Buck, 1997; Ryba and Tirindelli, 1997; Dulac and Torello, 2003; Shi and Zhang, 2007; Young and Trask, 2007; Liberles et al., 2009; Riviere et al., 2009; Liberles, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations documenting VR families.

claim: Vomeronasal sensory neurons (VSNs) encode information about gender, reproductive status, genetic background and individual differences.
source: The vomeronasal sensory neurons (VSNs) encode information about gender, reproductive status, genetic background and individual differences of animals of the same species, as well as that of heterospecifics (Halem et al., 1999; Holy et al., 2000; Boschat et al., 2002; Wyatt, 2003; Leinders-Zufall et al., 2004; Kimoto et al., 2005; Chamero et al., 2007; Kimoto et al., 2007; He et al., 2008; Haga et al., 2010; Papes et al., 2010; Isogai et al., 2011; Tolokh et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations documenting VSN response properties.

claim: The male-specific exocrine peptide ESP1 induces lordosis in female mice.
source: For example, the male-specific exocrine peptide ESP1 induces lordosis in female mice, a stereotypic gesture characterized by the arching of the back with raised rear, to signal receptivity to potential mates (Kimoto et al., 2005; Haga et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kimoto et al., 2005 and Haga et al., 2010.

claim: ESP1 induces lordosis through its receptor V2Rp5 (Vmn2r116), a member of the V2r family.
source: ESP1 induces lordosis through its receptor V2Rp5 (Vmn2r116), a member of the V2r family (Haga et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Haga et al., 2010.

claim: The activation of V2Rp5 receptor and its downstream neurons is sufficient to trigger lordosis.
source: In this case, the circuit that connects receptor-expressing neurons to brain centers appears to be a labeled line—the activation of a single receptor and its downstream neurons is sufficient to trigger lordosis, and removing the V2Rp5 receptor abolishes both the ESP1-evoked neural activation in the brain and the behavioral output of ESP1 (Haga et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Haga et al., 2010.

claim: Removing the V2Rp5 receptor abolishes both the ESP1-evoked neural activation in the brain and the behavioral output of ESP1.
source: In this case, the circuit that connects receptor-expressing neurons to brain centers appears to be a labeled line—the activation of a single receptor and its downstream neurons is sufficient to trigger lordosis, and removing the V2Rp5 receptor abolishes both the ESP1-evoked neural activation in the brain and the behavioral output of ESP1 (Haga et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Haga et al., 2010.

claim: There is a limited repertoire of highly stereotyped behavioral outputs resulting from VNO activation.
source: In contrast to the myriad sensory cues that induce behavioral responses and the large number of putative receptors, there is a limited repertoire of highly stereotyped behavioral outputs resulting from VNO activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations of VNO function and behavioral outputs.

claim: In genetic and surgical disruptions of VNO function, the onset and frequency of specific behaviors, but not the behavioral patterns per se, are altered.
source: In genetic and surgical disruptions of VNO function that lead to the alterations of innate behaviors, it is often observed that the onset and frequency of specific behaviors, but not the behavioral patterns per se, are altered.
evidence: This is based on observations from VNO disruption studies, representing established knowledge.

claim: Only a few receptors among the more than 300 members of the vomeronasal receptor families have been paired with ligands and assigned with functions.
source: Given that only a few receptors among the more than 300 members of the vomeronasal receptor families have been paired with ligands and assigned with functions (Boschat et al., 2002; Shi and Zhang, 2007; Young and Trask, 2007; Haga et al., 2010; Liberles, 2014), identification of receptors responding to specific pheromone signals should provide us with insights into the logic of information processing in the vomeronasal system.
evidence: This is supported by citations documenting the limited number of deorphanized receptors.

claim: The receptors for most pheromones have not been identified.
source: To date, despite advances in identifying pheromones (Kimoto et al., 2005; Chamero et al., 2007; Haga et al., 2010; Roberts et al., 2010; Ferrero et al., 2013), the receptors for most pheromones have not been identified.
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents the state of the field.

claim: The receptors conveying sex information remain elusive.
source: In particular, the receptors conveying sex information remain elusive.
evidence: This represents the gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Male mice exhibit robust mounting behaviors towards sexually mature females in the presence of estrus female urine.
source: Male mice exhibit robust mounting behaviors towards sexually mature females in the presence of estrus female urine (Dixon and Mackintosh, 1975; Ingersoll and Weinhold, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dixon and Mackintosh, 1975 and Ingersoll and Weinhold, 1987.

claim: Two populations of vomeronasal sensory neurons respond to gender and estrus status cues from female mouse urine.
source: In a previous study, we identified two populations of vomeronasal sensory neurons that respond to gender and estrus status cues from female mouse urine, respectively (He et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to He et al., 2008, a previous study by the authors.

claim: Males showed baseline mounting behavior toward ovariectomized females painted with vehicle or NEU.
source: Although males showed baseline mounting behavior toward ovariectomized females painted with vehicle or NEU (Figure 1A), the number of mounts and mounting duration increased significantly when the females were painted with EU (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The number of mounts and mounting duration increased significantly when ovariectomized females were painted with EU.
source: Although males showed baseline mounting behavior toward ovariectomized females painted with vehicle or NEU (Figure 1A), the number of mounts and mounting duration increased significantly when the females were painted with EU (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1A with statistical significance indicated.

claim: Estrous female urine contains cues that promote mounting behavior in male mice.
source: Thus, estrous female urine contains cues that promote mounting behavior in male mice.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the behavioral data showing increased mounting with EU.

claim: Sulfated steroids, including sulfated estrogens (SEs), have been shown to activate VSNs.
source: Sulfated steroids, including sulfated estrogens (SEs), have been shown to activate VSNs (Nodari et al., 2008; Meeks et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nodari et al., 2008 and Meeks et al., 2010.

claim: Estrus is marked by a surge in circulating estrogen.
source: Estrus is marked by a surge in circulating estrogen, which can be converted by specific enzymes to sulfated or glucuronidated estrogens (Blair, 2010) that are soluble and excreted in urine (Shackleton, 1986).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Blair, 2010 and Shackleton, 1986.

claim: Circulating estrogen can be converted by specific enzymes to sulfated or glucuronidated estrogens.
source: Estrus is marked by a surge in circulating estrogen, which can be converted by specific enzymes to sulfated or glucuronidated estrogens (Blair, 2010) that are soluble and excreted in urine (Shackleton, 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Blair, 2010.

claim: Sulfated or glucuronidated estrogens are soluble and excreted in urine.
source: Estrus is marked by a surge in circulating estrogen, which can be converted by specific enzymes to sulfated or glucuronidated estrogens (Blair, 2010) that are soluble and excreted in urine (Shackleton, 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shackleton, 1986.

claim: A population of VSNs responded robustly to EU but not NEU.
source: A population of VSNs responded robustly to EU but not NEU (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Two SEs, E1050 and E1103, exhibited overlapping response patterns.
source: Two SEs, 1, 3, 5(10)-estratrien-3, 17β-diol disulfate (E1050) and 1, 3, 5(10)-estratrien-3, 17β-diol 17-sulfate (E1103), exhibited overlapping response patterns (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: The majority of neurons activated by SEs were also activated by EU.
source: Remarkably, the majority of neurons activated by SEs were also activated by EU (Figure 1B–E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in multiple figures.

claim: EU activated >60% of SE-responding VSNs while NEU activated less than 10%.
source: EU activated >60% of SE-responding VSNs while NEU activated less than 10% (Figure 1D,E), suggesting that SE-responsive cells convey estrus information.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: SE-responsive cells convey estrus information.
source: EU activated >60% of SE-responding VSNs while NEU activated less than 10% (Figure 1D,E), suggesting that SE-responsive cells convey estrus information.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential activation by EU vs NEU.

claim: From cells responding to either E1050 or E1103, members of the V1rj clade of receptors were repeatedly identified.
source: From cells responding to either E1050 or E1103, we repeatedly identified members of the V1rj clade of receptors (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by single-cell RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: V1rj2 (Vmn1r89) was identified from 10 out of 15 SE-responding cells that yielded PCR products.
source: From these 15 cells, we identified V1rj2 (Vmn1r89) and V1rj3 (Vmn1r85) from 10 and 3 cells, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by single-cell RT-PCR data.

claim: V1rj3 (Vmn1r85) was identified from 3 out of 15 SE-responding cells that yielded PCR products.
source: From these 15 cells, we identified V1rj2 (Vmn1r89) and V1rj3 (Vmn1r85) from 10 and 3 cells, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by single-cell RT-PCR data.

claim: Vmn1r86 was found from one SE-responding cell.
source: Vmn1r86 (The sequence is identical to V1rj1 (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/nuccore/AY044668.1), but V1rj1 is not annotated in BLAT or Ensembl databases, nor was it linked to Vmn1r86.) was found from one cell.
evidence: This is supported by single-cell RT-PCR data.

claim: The V1rj members are located on mouse Chromosome 7 (Chr.7).
source: The V1rj members are located on mouse Chromosome 7 (Chr.7) and cluster into a single group in phylogenetic analysis (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on genomic annotation and phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: V1rj members cluster into a single group in phylogenetic analysis.
source: The V1rj members are located on mouse Chromosome 7 (Chr.7) and cluster into a single group in phylogenetic analysis (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: V1rj members share 55–86% amino acid identity and 81–95% similarity.
source: They share 55–86% amino acid identity and 81–95% similarity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: SEs at 100 nM concentration activated ∼10% of VSNs in control VNO slices.
source: SEs at 100 nM concentration activated ∼10% of VSNs in control VNO slices (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Significantly higher number of cells responded to 100 nM SEs in the V1rj2- and V1rj3-tdTomato-expressing VNOs.
source: Significantly higher number of cells responded to 100 nM SEs in the V1rj2- and V1rj3-tdTomato-expressing VNOs (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data comparing transgenic and control VNOs.

claim: V1rj2 and V1rj3 expressing VSNs showed dose-dependent activation, responding to the SEs at concentrations as low as 0.1 nM.
source: The V1rj2 and V1rj3 expressing VSNs showed dose-dependent activation, responding to the SEs at concentrations as low as 0.1 nM (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: V1rj2 was narrowly-tuned to sulfated estrogens but also responded to A7864.
source: Interestingly, while V1rj2 was narrowly-tuned to sulfated estrogens, it also responded to A7864, which had been previously shown to activate V1rj2 (Isogai et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by ligand specificity data and citation to Isogai et al., 2011.

claim: A7864 had been previously shown to activate V1rj2.
source: Interestingly, while V1rj2 was narrowly-tuned to sulfated estrogens, it also responded to A7864, which had been previously shown to activate V1rj2 (Isogai et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Isogai et al., 2011.

claim: V1rj3 showed more restricted tuning and was only activated by E1050 and E1103.
source: V1rj3, on the other hand, showed more restricted tuning and was only activated by E1050 and E1103.
evidence: This is supported by ligand specificity data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: EU strongly activated both V1rj2- and V1rj3-expressing VSNs while NEU activated them to a much lesser extent.
source: Importantly, EU strongly activated both V1rj2- and V1rj3-expressing VSNs while NEU activated them to a much lesser extent (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claim: V1rj3-expressing VSNs were more strongly activated by urine samples from estrous females under natural estrus cycle.
source: V1rj3-expressing VSNs were also more strongly activated by urine samples from estrous females under natural estrus cycle (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both V1rj2 and V1rj3 are receptors for the urinary cues enriched in EU that convey information about the estrus status of the female animals.
source: These results suggest that both V1rj2 and V1rj3 are receptors for the urinary cues enriched in EU that convey information about the estrus status of the female animals.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the differential activation by EU vs NEU in transgenic mice.

claim: Cues that activate the female urine specific cells (FUSCs) are present regardless of genetic background or estrus status of the donors.
source: In contrast, cues that activate the female urine specific cells (FUSCs) are present regardless of genetic background or estrus status of the donors (He et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to He et al., 2008.

claim: 7 out of the 10 FUSCs were found to express receptors belonging to the V1re clade.
source: 7 out of the 10 FUSCs were found to express receptors belonging to the V1re clade (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by single-cell RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The receptor genes identified from the FUSCs were all located on Chr.7.
source: Strikingly, the receptor genes identified from the FUSCs were all located on Chr.7 (referred to as V1re-Chr.7 receptors; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by genomic annotation and single-cell RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: None of V1re members located on Chr.17 was found in the FUSCs.
source: Despite their sequence similarity, none of V1re members located on Chr.17 was found in the FUSCs, whereas 5 out of 7 V1re-Chr.7 receptors were cloned from these cells.
evidence: This is supported by single-cell RT-PCR data.

claim: 5 out of 7 V1re-Chr.7 receptors were cloned from FUSCs.
source: Despite their sequence similarity, none of V1re members located on Chr.17 was found in the FUSCs, whereas 5 out of 7 V1re-Chr.7 receptors were cloned from these cells.
evidence: This is supported by single-cell RT-PCR data.

claim: The cloned V1re-Chr.7 receptors share 82–96% amino acid sequence similarity and 55–89% identity.
source: The cloned V1re-Chr.7 receptors share 82–96% amino acid sequence similarity and 55–89% identity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: V1re9 and V1re12-expressing cells were activated by all of the female but not the male urine samples.
source: When urine samples from males and females of several strains were applied to slices prepared from mice carrying all four alleles, tdTomato-expressing cells were activated by all of the female but not the male samples (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: V1re9 and V1re12-expressing cells were activated by the urine of females regardless of their estrous conditions.
source: Importantly, tdTomato-expressing cells were activated by the urine of females regardless of their estrous conditions (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: Urine from ovariectomized females can activate V1re9 and V1re12-expressing cells.
source: Urine from ovariectomized females can also activate V1re9 and V1re12-expressing cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Urine from ovariectomized females was less potent in activating V1re9 and V1re12-expressing neurons, especially the V1re9-expressing cells.
source: However, urine from ovariectomized females was less potent in activating these neurons, especially the V1re9-expressing cells.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data comparing responses to ovariectomized vs intact female urine.

claim: The expression of female-specific gender cue(s) was likely regulated by the ovaries.
source: These observations suggested that the expression of female-specific gender cue(s) was likely regulated by the ovaries.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced potency of ovariectomized female urine.

claim: V1re-Chr.7 receptors are activated by gender-specific cues from females.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that V1re-Chr.7 receptors are activated by gender-specific cues from females.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the selective activation by female urine across different conditions.

claim: There were no obvious differences between male and female VNOs in the numbers of cells expressing V1re9, e12, j2 and j3 receptors.
source: We did not find obvious differences between male and female VNOs in the numbers of cells expressing the receptors (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by double in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The patterns of response to E1050 or to EU were similar between VNOs obtained from male or female mice.
source: Consistent with this finding, the patterns of response to E1050 or to EU were similar between VNOs obtained from male or female mice (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: There is no obvious sexual dimorphism in detecting the female cues in the VNO.
source: Thus, there is no obvious sexual dimorphism in detecting the female cues in the VNO.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the lack of differences in receptor expression and response patterns between sexes.

claim: VSNs are extremely sensitive to their ligands; known ligands activate the VSNs at nanomolar or sub-nanomolar concentrations.
source: VSNs are extremely sensitive to their ligands; known ligands activate the VSNs at nanomolar or sub-nanomolar concentrations (Leinders-Zufall et al., 2000, 2004; Kimoto et al., 2005; He et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations documenting VSN sensitivity.

claim: One of the HPLC fractions, T16, strongly activated the V1re9 and V1re12 cells but not the V1rj2 or V1rj3 neurons.
source: One of the fractions, T16 (Figure 7A), strongly activated the V1re9 and V1re12 cells but not the V1rj2 or V1rj3 neurons (Figure 7B,C), suggesting that T16 contains the female gender-specific cue(s).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7B,C.

claim: T16 contains the female gender-specific cue(s).
source: One of the fractions, T16 (Figure 7A), strongly activated the V1re9 and V1re12 cells but not the V1rj2 or V1rj3 neurons (Figure 7B,C), suggesting that T16 contains the female gender-specific cue(s).
evidence: This is inferred from the selective activation of V1re9 and V1re12 by T16.

claim: 2-heptanone elicited strong EOG responses from the MOE.
source: As a control, we used 2-heptanone, which had been shown to activate neurons of the VNO and MOE. 2-heptanone elicited strong EOG responses (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is supported by EOG recording data shown in Figure 8A,B.

claim: SEs at 100 nM and 10 µM elicited only background level signals in EOG recordings from the MOE.
source: In contrast, SEs at 100 nM and 10 µM elicited only background level signals (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is supported by EOG recording data shown in Figure 8A,B.

claim: Neither pure nor diluted T16 fractions elicited EOG responses from the MOE.
source: Similarly, neither pure nor diluted T16 fractions elicited EOG responses (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by EOG recording data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: SEs and T16 do not activate the MOE.
source: Thus, these cues do not activate the MOE, demonstrating that the information is not processed by the main olfactory system.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the lack of EOG responses to SEs and T16.

claim: The information from SEs and T16 is not processed by the main olfactory system.
source: Thus, these cues do not activate the MOE, demonstrating that the information is not processed by the main olfactory system.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of MOE activation.

claim: Painting E1050 and E1103 on ovariectomized females did not increase mounting activities toward those females.
source: We painted E1050 and E1103 on ovariectomized females before exposing them to sexually-naïve males, but did not observe increased mounting activities toward those females.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assay data.

claim: The number of mounts and mounting duration with SE treatment were similar to those induced by vehicle or NEU treatment.
source: The number of mounts and mounting duration were similar to those induced by vehicle or NEU treatment (Figure 9A, Figure 9—figure supplement 1; also see Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 9A and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Supplementing NEU with SEs induced more robust mounting.
source: Interestingly, however, supplementing NEU with SEs induced more robust mounting (Figure 9—figure supplement 1), suggesting that additional cues besides the SEs were needed to elicit mounting behavior in males.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Additional cues besides the SEs were needed to elicit mounting behavior in males.
source: Interestingly, however, supplementing NEU with SEs induced more robust mounting (Figure 9—figure supplement 1), suggesting that additional cues besides the SEs were needed to elicit mounting behavior in males.
evidence: This is inferred from the synergistic effect of NEU+SE.

claim: Mixing T16 fraction with SEs induced mounting activities as robust as that induced by EU.
source: Indeed, mixing T16 fraction with SEs induced mounting activities as robust as that induced by EU (Figure 9A), whereas painting T16 fraction alone did not elicit increased mounting by males (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Painting T16 fraction alone did not elicit increased mounting by males.
source: Indeed, mixing T16 fraction with SEs induced mounting activities as robust as that induced by EU (Figure 9A), whereas painting T16 fraction alone did not elicit increased mounting by males (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Individually the female pheromone cues are not sufficient to induce mounting.
source: Thus, individually the female pheromone cues are not sufficient to induce mounting.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the behavioral data showing lack of effect of individual cues.

claim: The synergic action of both cues is required to promote male mounting behavior.
source: The synergic action of both cues is required to promote male mounting behavior.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the behavioral data showing synergistic effects.

claim: Conventional in situ hybridization techniques do not provide a clear distinction among highly homologous genes such as members of a given receptor clade.
source: However, conventional in situ hybridization techniques do not provide a clear distinction among highly homologous genes such as members of a given receptor clade.
evidence: This is a limitation of the technique based on established knowledge.

claim: In situ IEG staining is less sensitive than calcium imaging for measuring neuronal activation.
source: Moreover, in situ IEG staining is less sensitive than calcium imaging for measuring neuronal activation.
evidence: This is a comparison of methodological sensitivities based on knowledge.

claim: Neurons can be activated by 100 pM concentrations of E1103 or E1050.
source: Consistent with this, we found that the sulfated estrogen compounds activate the VSNs at sub-nanomolar concentrations: neurons can be activated by 100 pM concentrations of E1103 or E1050.
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data from calcium imaging experiments.

claim: The same sensitivity to SEs was recapitulated by the ectopically expressed V1rj2 and V1rj3 receptors.
source: Importantly, the same sensitivity was recapitulated by the ectopically expressed V1rj2 and V1rj3 receptors.
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data from transgenic mice expressing V1rj2 and V1rj3.

claim: The V1rj receptors are not only sensitive to sulfated steroids, but they are also highly selective.
source: The V1rj receptors are not only sensitive to sulfated steroids, but they are also highly selective.
evidence: This is supported by ligand specificity data showing selective responses.

claim: Except one sulfated androgen, none of the sulfated steroids other than estrogens activated the V1rj2 and V1rj3 receptors.
source: Except one sulfated androgen, none of the sulfated steroids other than estrogens activated the V1rj2 and V1rj3 receptors.
evidence: This is supported by ligand specificity data shown in Figure 3F,G.

claim: V1r receptors can discriminate distinct structural classes of steroids, while accepting minor structural variations within the class.
source: These observations indicate that V1r receptors can discriminate distinct structural classes of steroids, while accepting minor structural variations within the class.
evidence: This is inferred from the ligand specificity data.

claim: Receptors that recognize a given female cue are closely related family members belonging to the same clade of the V1r family.
